```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This tutorial searches for a public parks dataset, retrieves a small preview,
and charts one of its fields in base R. It assumes basic R skills; no mapping
software or knowledge of the publisher's data service is required. Run the
commands in order. Searching the package's catalog works offline; retrieving
records needs an internet connection. The publisher can change its data, so your
results may differ from another person's or from a later run. Allow about five
minutes, plus installation time if needed.

The examples below use a saved preview of 100 parks property records retrieved
on October 24, 2026 (Eastern time). You can use this historical snapshot offline
to reproduce the chart, or choose current records from the publisher in step 3.
The preview is not necessarily representative of all parks in Tampa or
Hillsborough County.

## 1. Install and load the package

Install the package from CRAN once (this needs an internet connection):

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tampaBayOpenData")
```

Load it each time you start a new R session:

```{r load-package, eval=TRUE}
library(tampaBayOpenData)
```

## 2. Find a dataset

Search for parks in the package's checked catalog:

```{r find-parks, eval=TRUE}
matches <- tbod_search_datasets("parks", source = "checked")
matches[, c("id", "title")]
```

Each row in these search results points to one dataset, with a title and an
`id` that you can use to retrieve it. `source = "checked"` searches the
package's built-in list of datasets whose structures have been inspected.
This search does not download park records. Find the `hillsborough-parks` row;
that is the ID we will use for the rest of this tutorial. The list can grow
when the package is updated.

## 3. Choose your parks data

Run one of the following options. Both create a table called `parks`, so
steps 4 and 5 work the same way with either source.

### Option A — Use saved example data (recommended for beginners)

Load the preview included with the installed package. Once the package is
installed, this needs no internet connection and reproduces the chart below.

```{r saved-parks}
parks_file <- system.file("extdata", "parks-preview.rds",
                          package = "tampaBayOpenData", mustWork = TRUE)
parks <- readRDS(parks_file)
```

`system.file()` finds the preview wherever R installed the package;
`readRDS()` loads the saved table into `parks`.

### Option B — Retrieve current parks data

With an internet connection, ask Hillsborough County's public service for up
to 100 current records instead. The chart may look different because the
publisher's records can change.

```{r retrieve-parks, eval=FALSE}
parks <- tbod_get_dataset("hillsborough-parks", limit = 100)
```

`tbod_get_dataset()` retrieves public records and puts them in `parks`, a
table you can explore in R. No account or password is needed. `limit = 100`
requests up to 100 records; if more match, these are only some of them. They
are the first records returned by the service, not a random sample. In this
source, each row describes a mapped property area managed by the county;
several rows can describe the same park. If retrieval fails, the package
reports an error; it does not substitute the saved preview.

The rendered tutorial always runs Option A and leaves Option B for you to run
manually. This keeps package builds offline, even when other tutorials are
configured to use live data.

## 4. Explore what you found

Look at the property name, type code, and use label, then count the rows you
received. These column names come from this dataset's checked schema.

```{r inspect-parks}
head(parks[, c("NAME", "TYPE", "USES")])
nrow(parks)
names(parks)
```

`head()` displays up to six property records with `NAME`, the source name;
`TYPE`, a source type code; and `USES`, a readable use label. `nrow()` gives
the size of your preview, while `names()` lists its available columns; do not
guess the meaning of a type code from its letters alone.

The `USES` column labels how each property is used. Which labels appear most
often in the records you received?

```{r count-uses}
uses <- trimws(parks$USES)
uses[is.na(uses) | uses == ""] <- "Not reported"
park_uses <- table(uses)
park_uses <- sort(park_uses, decreasing = TRUE)
park_uses
```

The first two lines group missing or blank labels as "Not reported";
`table()` counts each label and `sort()` puts the largest counts first. These counts describe
only the returned preview; they do not tell you how many parks of each type
exist across the county.

## 5. Make your first chart

Show the five most common use labels in that same preview:

```{r chart-uses, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Horizontal bars counting property records for up to five most common use labels in the parks preview."}
top_uses <- head(park_uses, 5)
par(mar = c(4, 10, 3, 1))
if (length(top_uses) > 0) {
  barplot(rev(top_uses), horiz = TRUE, las = 1, cex.names = 0.8,
        col = "steelblue", xlab = "Property records",
        main = "Most common uses in this preview")
} else {
  plot.new()
  text(0.5, 0.5, "No property records returned")
}
```

The code selects up to five labels and places the largest count at the top;
the left margin leaves room for the labels. If no records are returned, it
shows a message instead of bars.

Each bar counts property records with one of the publisher's use labels;
a longer bar means more records in that category. In the saved preview,
Sports has the most records, followed by Nature; your current preview may differ.
Categories outside the top five are omitted, so the bars may not add up to 100.
The chart is a quick look at the rows you loaded, not an estimate for all
county parks. The first 100 records may change, and mapped property outlines
do not establish legal boundaries, public access, or opening hours. If the
service is temporarily unavailable, try the retrieval again later; the
[retrieval guide's troubleshooting section](retrieval.html#troubleshooting-common-errors)
has more help. If the publisher changes the column names, retrieval may stop
with a schema error; check the source before adapting this example.

Data: [Hillsborough County Parks and Recreation properties](https://hillsborough.maps.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=96d17f4369f14bc5b283d8863b016373),
used under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
The chart counts records, not unique parks, park area, quality, or demand.

## What to try next

To work with another dataset, change the search word, choose an `id` from the
results, and inspect `names()` before counting a column. The [discovery
guide](discovery.html) helps you find more datasets;
the [retrieval guide](retrieval.html) covers filters and larger downloads.
When you are ready for maps, try the [spatial example](mapping-capital-improvements.html).
For longer real-world walkthroughs, see [housing](housing-development.html),
[water quality](water-quality.html), and
[infrastructure](infrastructure-projects.html).
